classification.difficultyReason: Identify each instrument's unit, infer the value of unlabelled intervals from labelled graduations, and read the indicated tick; the hardest scale requires dividing a 200 mL span into four intervals.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly assesses reading whole-number and decimal measurements across length, mass and capacity. Decimal length equivalence is the closest available primary catalogue skill; mass and capacity equivalence cover the other scales.
questions.methodNote: Identify the scale unit and the value of each interval, then read the indicated measurement. Pages 2–5 establish measurement units and powers-of-ten relationships; no distinct scale-reading demonstration is supplied.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read labelled measuring scales and their subdivisions, including decimal readings.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct capacity conversions using factors of 1000.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts assess conversion between capacity units.
questions.methodNote: The capacity table on page 2 and conversion arrows on page 3 give 1000 mL = 1 L and 1000 L = 1 kL. Multiply or divide by 1000 as appropriate.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct capacity conversions using factors of 1000.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert the target kilometre to metres, then interpret the lap count as the total distance divided by the distance per lap.

questions.mappingNote: Applies the length conversions in the unit table and Example 1 to a repeated-distance problem.
questions.methodNote: Use 1 km = 1000 m, multiplying kilometres by 1000 before calculating in metres.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert kilometres to metres, then divide by the length of one lap.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert masses to a common unit, multiply two quantities, add and express the total in two units.

questions.mappingNote: Uses Example 3's conversions in both directions and Example 4's combination of masses after conversion.
questions.methodNote: Multiply kilograms by 1000 to obtain grams; divide grams by 1000 to obtain kilograms. Combine masses in a common unit.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert masses to a common unit, multiply two quantities, add and express the total in two units.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguish the number of equal gaps from the number of markers, including both endpoints.

questions.mappingNote: Uses the kilometre-to-metre conversion in Example 1. The distinction between gaps and endpoints follows from this question's first-to-last wording.
questions.methodNote: Convert kilometres to metres before dividing by the spacing; count both endpoint markers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Distinguish the number of equal gaps from the number of markers, including both endpoints.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert units, subtract the picture width and divide the remaining wall width equally.

questions.mappingNote: Uses the metre-to-centimetre conversion in the unit table and Example 1; equal side gaps follow from the picture being centred.
questions.methodNote: Multiply metres by 100 to obtain centimetres, then calculate in the common unit.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert units, subtract the picture width and divide the remaining wall width equally.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct multiplication and division of measurements by whole numbers, retaining the given units.

questions.mappingNote: Question 11 directly assesses multiplication and division of numerical measurements, rather than conversion between units. Worked answers use ordinary decimal arithmetic and retain each original unit.
questions.methodNote: The supplied teaching establishes metric units and shows arithmetic with measurement quantities while retaining units. It does not demonstrate general decimal multiplication or division.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct multiplication and division of measurements by whole numbers, retaining the given units.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate costs from unit prices, converting quantities to the priced unit where necessary.

questions.mappingNote: Question 12 continues Exercise 9A. Pages 2–5 establish length, mass and capacity conversions; page 8 also demonstrates multiplying a unit cost by a quantity. The 9B material on pages 7–8 is reference evidence only.
questions.methodNote: Convert the measured quantity to the unit used by the price, using the metric conversion factor, then multiply by the price per unit.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate costs from unit prices, converting quantities to the priced unit where necessary.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine the centi- and micro- prefix factors to convert one centimetre to micrometres.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly assesses combining the centi- and micro- prefix factors for length, so measurement-prefixes is the closest primary skill.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–3 teach conversion using equivalent units and multiplication or division by powers of ten. Page 7 defines a micrometre as one millionth of a metre and centi- as one hundredth; Example 5 on pages 7–8 demonstrates staged conversion using unit equivalences.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine the centi- and micro- prefix factors to convert one centimetre to micrometres.

classification.difficultyReason: Find half the stated capacity and convert a large quantity from megalitres to litres.

questions.mappingNote: The question requires half the capacity followed by the same megalitre-to-litre conversion taught in Example 5. Capacity conversion is the primary assessed skill, supported by the meaning of mega-.
questions.methodNote: The metric conversion table gives 1 megalitre as 1,000,000 litres. Example 5 on page 7 converts megalitres to litres by multiplying by 1,000,000; its continuation on page 8 then converts litres to millilitres.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find half the stated capacity and convert a large quantity from megalitres to litres.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert kilometres to micrometres using two metric prefix factors.

questions.mappingNote: The task requires applying kilo and micro prefix factors to a length, so measurement-prefixes is the closest directly assessed skill, supported by metric length conversion.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–3 teach metric conversions by multiplying or dividing by powers of ten. Page 7 defines a micrometre as one millionth of a metre and gives kilo as a factor of 1000. Example 5 on pages 7–8 demonstrates conversion through the basic unit in two stages.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert kilometres to micrometres using two metric prefix factors.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine the mega prefix with successive mass conversions from tonnes to milligrams.

questions.mappingNote: The unfamiliar mega prefix is the most advanced directly assessed knowledge; ordinary mass-unit conversions complete the task.
questions.methodNote: Page 7 defines mega as one million. Example 5 on pages 7–8 demonstrates successive conversions by multiplying the quantity by the appropriate factors. Pages 2–3 establish the mass conversion factors of 1000 between tonnes, kilograms, grams and milligrams.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine the mega prefix with successive mass conversions from tonnes to milligrams.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the deci- and centi- prefixes to convert a length by dividing by 10.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly assesses interpreting the deci- prefix and converting centimetres to decimetres, so measurement-prefixes is the closest catalogue match.
questions.methodNote: Page 7 defines deci- as one tenth and centi- as one hundredth, giving 10 centimetres per decimetre. Pages 2–3 teach conversion using unit equivalences and division when converting to a larger unit; Example 5 on pages 7–8 applies prefix factors.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use the deci- and centi- prefixes to convert a length by dividing by 10.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert millilitres to litres, then apply the supplied litre–cubic decimetre equivalence.

questions.mappingNote: The question supplies the equivalence between litres and cubic decimetres; converting millilitres to litres and applying that equivalence directly assesses volume–capacity conversion.
questions.methodNote: The unit table and conversion arrows establish 1000 millilitres per litre. Example 5 converts capacity in successive stages using the relevant unit equivalences.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert millilitres to litres, then apply the supplied litre–cubic decimetre equivalence.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the micro prefix to a century, then convert the supplied number of days into minutes.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly assesses applying the micro prefix to a time quantity, followed by conversion from days to minutes using the supplied century length.
questions.methodNote: Page 7 defines micro- as one millionth and Example 5 uses successive unit conversions, continued on page 8. Page 2 supplies 24 hours per day and 60 minutes per hour; page 3 illustrates multiplication and division by conversion factors.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the micro prefix to a century, then convert the supplied number of days into minutes.

classification.difficultyReason: Find the mass of one block by division, then multiply by three.

questions.mappingNote: Divide 1875 g by 5 to find one block's mass, then multiply by 3. This directly applies the taught unitary method.
questions.methodNote: The introduction on page 8 and Example 6 on page 9 divide the given quantity by the number of items to obtain one item's value, then multiply by the required number.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find the mass of one block by division, then multiply by three.

classification.difficultyReason: Find the cost of one kilogram, then multiply by four, directly following the unitary-method examples.

questions.mappingNote: Divide the cost of 3 kg of tea by 3 to find the cost of 1 kg, then multiply by 4. This directly assesses the taught unitary method.
questions.methodNote: Page 8 finds the cost of one apple by division, then multiplies by the requested number. Example 6 on page 9 follows the same sequence for cans of drink.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find the cost of one kilogram, then multiply by four, directly following the unitary-method examples.

classification.difficultyReason: Find the mass for one tin, scale to three tins, then convert grams to kilograms.

questions.mappingNote: Divide the given mass by seven to obtain one tin's capacity, multiply by three, and divide by 1000 to express the result in kilograms. Page 32 concerns time and is not needed for this question.
questions.methodNote: Page 8 introduces finding one unit by division and multiplying by the required number; Example 6 on page 9 repeats this method. Pages 2–3 establish that 1000 grams equal 1 kilogram and conversion to a larger metric unit uses division.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find the mass for one tin, scale to three tins, then convert grams to kilograms.

classification.difficultyReason: Find the distance travelled on one litre, then multiply by the required number of litres.

questions.mappingNote: Divide 77 km by 11 to obtain the distance on one litre, then multiply by 130. This directly applies the taught unitary method to fuel use; no unit conversion is needed.
questions.methodNote: Page 8 introduces finding the value of one unit before multiplying by the required quantity. Example 6 on page 9 demonstrates division followed by multiplication.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find the distance travelled on one litre, then multiply by the required number of litres.

classification.difficultyReason: Find the distance travelled in one hour, then multiply by eight, using whole-number arithmetic.

questions.mappingNote: Question 5 applies this unitary method to distance: divide the distance for three hours by three, then multiply the one-hour distance by eight. No time-unit conversion is required.
questions.methodNote: Page 8 introduces finding one unit by division and then multiplying by the requested number of units. Example 6 on page 9 demonstrates the same division-then-multiplication sequence.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find the distance travelled in one hour, then multiply by eight, using whole-number arithmetic.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that different pack sizes require a common cost per orange, calculate both unit prices, and compare them while retaining the fractional-cent value.

questions.mappingNote: Divide each offer's total price by its number of oranges, then compare the exact costs per orange. This directly assesses best buys through the unitary method.
questions.methodNote: Page 8 finds the cost of one apple by division; Example 6 on page 9 similarly divides the total cost by the number of cans before scaling.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find and compare two unit prices using the taught unitary method.

classification.difficultyReason: Find the distance for one second, scale to 30 minutes and convert metres to kilometres.

questions.mappingNote: Find the distance travelled in one second by dividing 100 m by 15, multiply by 1800 seconds, then divide metres by 1000 to obtain kilometres. This directly applies the exercise's unitary method with supporting unit conversions.
questions.methodNote: Page 8 introduces finding the value for one unit before multiplying by the required quantity; Example 6 on page 9 demonstrates this sequence. Pages 2–3 establish metric length conversions, and pages 2 and 32 establish 60 seconds per minute.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find the distance for one second, scale to 30 minutes and convert metres to kilometres.

classification.difficultyReason: Express an hour as 60 minutes, find distance per minute from the given pair, and scale to 60 minutes at the intended constant pace.

questions.mappingNote: Find the distance walked in one minute by dividing 200 m by 2, then multiply by 60 for one hour, assuming the same walking pace as intended by the unitary-method exercise.
questions.methodNote: Page 8 introduces finding the value for one unit before multiplying by the required number of units; Example 6 on page 9 demonstrates this sequence. Pages 2 and 32 state that 60 minutes equal one hour.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert one hour to minutes, find the distance walked in one minute, then multiply by 60.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert metres to centimetres, find the cost of one centimetre and scale to the required length.

questions.mappingNote: The rope question applies the same unitary cost method after converting 2 m to 200 cm. Its most advanced directly assessed skill is the unitary method.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–3 establish metric length conversions. Page 8 introduces finding the value of one unit before multiplying; Example 6 on page 9 demonstrates dividing the known cost by the known quantity, then multiplying by the required quantity. Page 32 concerns time conversions and is not needed here.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert metres to centimetres, find the cost of one centimetre and scale to the required length.

classification.difficultyReason: Find distance per second using the unitary method, scale to a minute and an hour, and express the longer distance in kilometres.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts apply the taught unitary method to distance and time. Divide the given distance by 10 to find distance in one second, then multiply by the required duration in seconds.
questions.methodNote: Page 8 introduces finding one unit first by division, then multiplying by the required number of units; Example 6 on page 9 repeats this sequence. Pages 2 and 32 establish time conversions, while pages 2–3 establish metre–kilometre conversion.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find distance per second using the unitary method, scale to a minute and an hour, and express the longer distance in kilometres.

classification.difficultyReason: Find the mass per apricot, scale to 20 apricots, and convert the resulting grams to the requested kilograms.

questions.mappingNote: The apricot task directly applies the taught unitary method to mass, followed by the taught metric conversion.
questions.methodNote: Page 8 introduces finding one item's value before multiplying by the required number; Example 6 on page 9 demonstrates this sequence. Pages 2–3 establish 1000 grams equals 1 kilogram and division by 1000 to convert grams to kilograms. Page 32 concerns time and is not needed for this question.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find the mass of one apricot, multiply by 20 and convert grams to kilograms.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that increasing the number of workers decreases completion time, then calculate through one worker.

questions.mappingNote: Question 12 requires inverse variation: one man takes 63 × 9 days and 40 men take that time divided by 40. The solution uses a one-worker intermediate, but original teaching evidence for the inverse relationship remains missing.
questions.methodNote: Pages 8 and 9 teach finding the value for one unit before scaling to the requested number. Their examples concern direct proportion. Pages 2, 3 and 32 provide measurement and time conversions but no inverse worker-count/completion-time demonstration.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise that increasing the number of workers decreases completion time, then calculate through one worker.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the demonstrated divide-to-one then multiply method to seedling prices; the changing quantities and totals require selecting the correct divisor and multiplier but no new strategy.

questions.mappingNote: Both seedling tasks use the same direct unitary method: divide each given total cost by its seedling count, then multiply by the requested count. Measurement and time conversions on pages 2, 3 and 32 are not required.
questions.methodNote: The introduction on page 8 finds the cost of one apple before multiplying by the required quantity. Example 6 on page 9 divides the total cost by 12, then multiplies the unit cost by 7.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find the cost of one seedling by division, then multiply by the required number, directly following Example 6.

classification.difficultyReason: Measure each printed boundary side with a ruler to millimetre precision, then add the measurements; both the measurement method and actual-size printing are explicitly directed.

questions.mappingNote: Both figures assess physical ruler measurement before perimeter addition; numerical measurements cannot be established from the raster without its physical page scale.
questions.methodNote: Measure every boundary side in millimetres and add the lengths, following the perimeter addition method in Example 7.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Measure each side with a ruler and add the measurements.

classification.difficultyReason: Count unit boundary lengths, including the two inward notches in part c.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b apply boundary addition to rectangles on a unit grid. Part c applies the same method to a concave boundary, retaining every notch edge.
questions.methodNote: Page 10 defines perimeter as the sum of boundary lengths and demonstrates counting 1 cm intervals. Example 7 on page 11 adds all sides of a concave rectilinear figure.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Count unit boundary lengths, including the two inward notches in part c.

classification.difficultyReason: Add the four side lengths of a rectangle using the given decimal dimensions.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly apply the taught side-sum method to rectangular rooms with decimal dimensions.
questions.methodNote: Page 10 defines perimeter as the sum of side lengths and demonstrates adding all four rectangle sides. Example 7 on page 11 likewise adds each boundary length.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Add the four side lengths of a rectangle using the given decimal dimensions.

classification.difficultyReason: Add the labelled side lengths, use equal-side markings and collect like terms.

questions.mappingNote: Each part adds boundary lengths; parts b–f simplify like terms, and c and f additionally use the printed equal-side markings. Collecting like terms is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 10 defines perimeter as the sum of side lengths and demonstrates 3a+3a+2b=6a+2b. Example 7 on page 11 adds every boundary side.

questions.methodNote: Page 10 defines perimeter as the sum of boundary side lengths and demonstrates adding all four rectangle sides. Page 11 Example 7 adds every boundary side.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct two distinct rectangles for each perimeter, including a perimeter requiring decimal side lengths.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct three different rectangles for each fixed perimeter, choosing different pairs of side lengths.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that the staircase's horizontal and vertical segments sum to the given total width and height.

questions.mappingNote: Apply the taught boundary-sum method, first recognising that the staircase's rightward and downward segments total the given width and height. The directly assessed skill is composite perimeter.
questions.methodNote: Page 10 defines perimeter as the sum of boundary side lengths. Example 7 on page 11 adds every side of an orthogonal concave polygon.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise that the staircase's horizontal and vertical segments sum to the given total width and height.

classification.difficultyReason: Count the unit cells within each marked rectangle, optionally organising the count by rows, and report the total in square centimetres as instructed.

questions.mappingNote: This question directly assesses counting square-centimetre cells inside rectangles; worked responses retain counting by rows rather than replacing the requested method with formula substitution.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Count unit squares inside four rectangles on a shared grid.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert standard area units using square side lengths and the hectare equivalence.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts assess area-unit conversion; part b additionally uses the explicitly taught hectare and square-kilometre equivalence.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert standard area units using square side lengths and the hectare equivalence.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert the width from kilometres to metres before applying the rectangle area formula.

questions.methodNote: Use matching length units, then calculate area as length multiplied by width. Example 11 demonstrates converting a dimension before substitution.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert the width from kilometres to metres before applying the rectangle area formula.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret which quantity is missing in each table row and choose multiplication for area or division of area by the known side for a missing dimension.

questions.mappingNote: Row a directly applies the rectangle formula; rows b–d invert that same formula to find a missing dimension.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate a rectangular area, then multiply by the cost per square metre.

questions.methodNote: The Area summary and Example 11 use area = length × width with measurements in consistent units.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate a rectangular wall's area and account for two coats of paint.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert both dimensions to metres, calculate the rectangular area and apply the cost per square metre.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert both dimensions to metres, calculate the rectangular area and apply the cost per square metre.

classification.difficultyReason: Add hours, minutes and seconds, regroup across units and midnight, and express mixed time notations using a.m. or p.m.

questions.mappingNote: Every part finds a finish time from a starting time and duration, so calculate-elapsed-time is the closest primary skill. Part d additionally converts a supplied 24-hour time; parts b, c and e require crossing midnight or regrouping.
questions.methodNote: Use the a.m./p.m. and 24-hour conventions on page 32, add time as in Example 22, and build up to whole minutes or hours as in Examples 23–24 and the Time summary. Regroup using 60 seconds per minute and 60 minutes per hour.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Add hours, minutes and seconds, regroup across units and midnight, and express mixed time notations using a.m. or p.m.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert a mixed mass to grams and use the unitary method to compare prices for an equal mass.

questions.mappingNote: The question applies the unitary method after converting 1 kg 50 g to 1050 g, comparing equal-mass prices to determine the best buy.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–3 establish metric mass conversion. Page 8 introduces the unitary method: divide to find the cost of one unit, then multiply to find the cost of the required quantity.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert a mixed mass to grams and use the unitary method to compare prices for an equal mass.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify all six triangles and compare their areas using their common perpendicular height and different base lengths.

questions.mappingNote: The task assesses triangle-area comparison using a common altitude, so area-of-triangle is the primary skill.
questions.methodNote: The triangle-area teaching derives area as one half of base times perpendicular height, including triangles whose altitude falls outside the triangle. Compare bases when the perpendicular height is common.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify all six triangles and compare their areas using their common perpendicular height and different base lengths.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the longest side as the hypotenuse and use the other two sides as the perpendicular base and height in the triangle-area formula.

questions.mappingNote: This question directly assesses triangle area after identifying the two shorter sides of a right-angled triangle as perpendicular base and height.
questions.methodNote: The triangle-area teaching derives and applies A = 1/2 × base × perpendicular height.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the two perpendicular sides from the three given lengths and apply the triangle area formula.

classification.difficultyReason: Scale a grazing requirement and convert hectares to square metres before determining the supported flock.

questions.mappingNote: Both responses assess proportional scaling from the shared 200 m² for 3 sheep; the second also requires the taught hectare conversion. Unitary-method ratios is the closest directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 14 defines one hectare as 10 000 square metres. Use multiplication and division to scale the given grazing requirement, retaining exact arithmetic.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Scale a grazing requirement and convert hectares to square metres before determining the supported flock.

classification.difficultyReason: Use five equal sides to calculate perimeter, then convert the result from millimetres to metres.

questions.mappingNote: The question combines a regular polygon perimeter with a change of length units, making length and perimeter problems the closest assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 10 calculates perimeter by summing side lengths. Pages 2–3 establish that converting millimetres to metres requires division by 1000.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate the perimeter of five equal sides and convert millimetres to metres.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate distance directly from speed and time in compatible units.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly assesses the same distance calculation as Example 27, with no unit conversion.
questions.methodNote: Page 36 defines speed as distance divided by time. Page 37 Example 27 explicitly calculates distance as speed multiplied by time, using metres per second and seconds.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate distance directly from speed and time in compatible units.

classification.difficultyReason: Divide the given distance by the elapsed time; units already match.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly assesses calculating speed from distance and time, with no unit conversion required.
questions.methodNote: Example 26 divides distance by time. The average-speed explanation and Example 28 apply this method to average speed and retain exact fractional arithmetic.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Divide the given distance by the elapsed time; units already match.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate speed by dividing a mixed-number distance by a fractional time.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly assesses speed from distance and time; fraction division supports the calculation.
questions.methodNote: Page 37, Example 28, calculates cycling speed as distance divided by fractional hours, then multiplies by the reciprocal. Examples 26 and 29 establish the speed–distance–time relationship.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate speed by dividing a mixed-number distance by a fractional time.

classification.difficultyReason: Infer missing dimensions and subtract rectangular or triangular areas from enclosing rectangles.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts assess composite area by subtraction; part a subtracts a rectangular opening and part b subtracts a right triangle from an enclosing rectangle.
questions.methodNote: Rectangle area is length times width. Pages 17–19 teach subtracting an opening from an enclosing rectangle, including a uniformly thick frame. Pages 21–23 establish triangle area as half base times perpendicular height.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Infer missing dimensions and subtract rectangular or triangular areas from enclosing rectangles.

classification.difficultyReason: Multiply the common side length by the six sides of a regular hexagon.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly assesses the perimeter of a regular polygon using its given side length.
questions.methodNote: The perimeter teaching defines perimeter as the sum of all side lengths. Six equal sides may be summed by multiplication.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Multiply the common side length by the six sides of a regular hexagon.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate the distances of two stages and divide their sum by the total journey time.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed skill is average speed over a journey containing stages at different speeds.
questions.methodNote: Page 37 demonstrates distance = speed × time and speed = distance ÷ time, and explains average speed. Page 38 Example 29 applies speed × time to a journey distance. Calculate both stage distances, then divide their total by the five-hour journey time.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate the distances of two stages and divide their sum by the total journey time.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert a mixed time interval to hours, calculate distance, then combine distances and times for an entire journey.

questions.mappingNote: Part a calculates distance after converting minutes to hours. Part b assesses average speed over the complete two-stage journey, so average-speed-journey is the primary skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 gives 60 minutes = 1 hour. Page 37 teaches distance = speed × time and average speed = distance ÷ time, including fractional hours; page 38 reinforces distance calculations using average speed.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert a mixed time interval to hours, calculate distance, then combine distances and times for an entire journey.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine four supplied imperial conversion factors, then convert centimetres to kilometres.

questions.mappingNote: The question supplies the imperial conversion facts and directly assesses a sequence of length conversions ending in kilometres.
questions.methodNote: Use equivalent lengths successively. The supplied metric table and conversion arrows establish division by 100 from centimetres to metres and division by 1000 from metres to kilometres.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine four supplied imperial conversion factors, then convert centimetres to kilometres.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise the triangle's perpendicular height from the square, then subtract its area from the square's area.

questions.mappingNote: Subtract the central triangle's area from the square's area. Composite area is the closest supplied skill; the square's opposite sides determine the triangle's perpendicular height.
questions.methodNote: Pages 13–14 establish rectangle and square area; page 17 introduces subtracting a smaller area from a larger one. Pages 21–23 establish triangle area as half base times perpendicular height, including choosing a differently oriented base.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise the triangle's perpendicular height from the square, then subtract its area from the square's area.

classification.difficultyReason: Build up across several days and combine hours, minutes and seconds.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly assesses elapsed time across several days, with the final duration expressed in hours, minutes and seconds.
questions.methodNote: Use the 60-second, 60-minute and 24-hour relationships. Build up to whole minutes, hours and days as demonstrated in Examples 23–25.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Build up across several days and combine hours, minutes and seconds.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert tonnes to kilograms and divide the elephant's mass by one person's lifting capacity; the exact quotient needs no rounding decision.

questions.mappingNote: Convert the elephant's mass to kilograms before dividing by the given lifting capacity; this directly assesses a mass problem involving different units.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 gives 1000 kilograms = 1 tonne. Pages 2–3 teach converting metric units by multiplying or dividing by the appropriate power of 10.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert tonnes to kilograms, then divide by the mass one person can lift.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate the area using the perpendicular legs, then recognise the same area with BC as a different base and reverse the area formula to find AX; part a supplies the intermediate area.

questions.mappingNote: Part a directly assesses triangle area. Part b assesses finding an unknown perpendicular height from the same area, so find-unknown-side-from-area is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: The triangle teaching identifies a perpendicular base-height pair and establishes area = one half × base × height. Apply that formula first with AB and AC, then with BC and AX, using inverse operations to recover the height.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate one triangle's area using its perpendicular sides, then use a different base and the same area to determine its perpendicular height.

classification.difficultyReason: Combines direct volume calculation, inverse use of the volume formula with mixed units, and recovery of dimensions from three face areas.

questions.mappingNote: Part a directly assesses rectangular-prism volume; part b reverses V = Ah after converting the height to millimetres; part c reconstructs mutually consistent dimensions from the authorised three face areas before calculating volume.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–3 establish metric length conversions. Page 29 derives V = lwh and Example 20 substitutes dimensions before multiplying. Page 30 establishes V = Ah and permits any face as the base. Part c applies these rectangular-face relationships using factor pairs, then the taught volume formula.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines direct volume calculation, inverse use of the volume formula with mixed units, and recovery of dimensions from three face areas.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret the micro prefix, build two separate chains of time conversions, and compare their numerical counts to judge the claim.

questions.mappingNote: The question principally assesses chained time-unit conversions and comparison; identifying micro as one millionth supports the first conversion. The supplied teaching pages do not explicitly define the micro prefix, so the worked answer supplies that definition.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–3 explain metric prefixes and multiplication or division by conversion factors. Page 32 gives 60 seconds per minute, 60 minutes per hour and 24 hours per day; Example 21 converts time by multiplying the relevant factors.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines microsecond and century conversions to compare two large counts.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose a common area and construct three figures satisfying it while deliberately varying and checking their perimeters; dimensions and construction choices are unsupplied.

questions.mappingNote: Constructing and checking equal-area figures with distinct boundary lengths directly assesses the relationship between area and perimeter. The sample includes both rectangles and a triangle.
questions.methodNote: Page 10 calculates perimeter by summing boundary sides; page 13 calculates rectangle area as length times width; page 17 includes constructing rectangles of a specified area; page 21 derives triangle area as half the enclosing rectangle's area.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct three figures satisfying equal-area and different-perimeter constraints, then verify both properties.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose a common perimeter, construct three compatible figures, and verify that their areas differ, coordinating boundary-length and area constraints without supplied dimensions.

questions.mappingNote: Construct two rectangles with the same sum of adjacent sides and a 3–4–5 right triangle having that perimeter, then compare areas using the taught rectangle and triangle methods.
questions.methodNote: Page 11 finds perimeter by adding side lengths. Pages 17–18 use rectangle dimensions and rectangle areas; page 21 derives triangle area as half the enclosing rectangle's area.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct three figures meeting a common perimeter constraint and demonstrate that their areas differ.

classification.difficultyReason: Infer the dimensions of a square-cornered offset boundary and combine composite areas with perimeter.

questions.mappingNote: The garden and its square-cornered path require composite rectangle subtraction, with perimeter as a secondary assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 11 Example 7 adds boundary lengths for composite perimeter. Page 13 teaches rectangle area as length times width. Page 17 introduces adding rectangle areas or subtracting smaller areas from a larger area.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Infer the dimensions of a square-cornered offset boundary and combine composite areas with perimeter.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret two relative-day descriptions and count forwards through the week.

questions.mappingNote: The closest catalogue skill is duration-problems because the task combines relative-day intervals. Pages 2–3 cover measurement conventions; page 32 supplies the relevant days-and-weeks context.
questions.methodNote: Count forwards by whole days, using the seven-day week stated on page 32. First determine tomorrow and today, then count three days after yesterday.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interpret two relative-day descriptions and count forwards through the week.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare package prices and combine whole packages and individual cards to maximise the number within a fixed budget.

questions.mappingNote: The unitary-method introduction on page 8 and Example 6 on page 9 support comparing card prices. Whole-package combinations extend that method to the fixed-budget challenge.
questions.methodNote: Find the cost of one item by dividing the total cost by the number of items; compare prices and use multiplication to calculate purchase costs.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare package prices and combine whole packages and individual cards to maximise the number within a fixed budget.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine workforce, duration and distance at a constant working rate, then round the required workforce up to a whole person.

questions.mappingNote: The task requires compound direct and inverse variation. Its authored solution extends the local unitary method to kilometres per person per day, then rounds the workforce upward.
questions.methodNote: Pages 8–9 teach the unitary method: determine the amount for one unit before scaling. Pages 36–38 demonstrate constant rates and distance per unit time. No inspected worked demonstration explicitly combines people, days and completed work.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine workforce, duration and distance at a constant working rate, then round the required workforce up to a whole person.

classification.difficultyReason: Systematically enumerate repeated-digit displays while respecting valid hours and minutes.

questions.mappingNote: Reading and constraining 24-hour displays is the directly assessed measurement skill; systematic listing supplies the challenge reasoning.
questions.methodNote: Page 32 explains the 24-hour system, midnight and 60 minutes per hour. Enumerate valid clock displays using these limits and the question's explicit unpadded-hour format.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Systematically enumerate repeated-digit displays while respecting valid hours and minutes.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine overlapping pair measurements, recognise that the baby is counted twice, and halve the remaining mass.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed reasoning combines addition, subtraction and halving with all measurements already in kilograms; multistep arithmetic is the closest supplied skill. The authored solution explains the double counting directly rather than introducing simultaneous equations.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–3 establish kilogram notation and metric mass units. Pages 8–9 demonstrate arithmetic reasoning through a unit quantity. None of these inspected pages explicitly demonstrates recovering an individual mass from overlapping pair measurements.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine overlapping pair measurements, recognise that the baby is counted twice, and halve the remaining mass.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert lengths to common units, distinguish plants from intervals, and multiply by the number of rows.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed task combines metric length conversion with counting equally spaced positions along a measured length.
questions.methodNote: Use 100 centimetres per metre to express all lengths in centimetres. Remove the two end margins, divide by the spacing to count intervals, add one to count plants, then multiply by 12 rows.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert lengths to common units, distinguish plants from intervals, and multiply by the number of rows.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguish stops from intervals, then find one interval and multiply by eight.

questions.mappingNote: Treat each equal gap as one unit. The first-to-third distance covers two gaps; nine stops create eight gaps.
questions.methodNote: Page 8 introduces the unitary method: divide to find one unit, then multiply by the required number of units.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Distinguish stops from intervals, then find one interval and multiply by eight.

classification.difficultyReason: Count leap days across nineteen years and interpret the remainder after division by seven.

questions.mappingNote: Duration problems is the closest supplied skill; interpreting the remainder after division by seven directly supports the weekday calculation. Leap-year reasoning requires additional original teaching evidence.
questions.methodNote: Page 32 states that a week contains seven days and demonstrates time conversion with remainders. Pages 33–34 demonstrate elapsed-time calculations. These inspected pages do not teach leap-year counting or calendar weekday calculations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Count leap days across nineteen years and interpret the remainder after division by seven.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that equal distances at different speeds take unequal times, introduce a convenient common distance despite none being given, and calculate total distance divided by total time.

questions.mappingNote: Apply the taught distance/time definition to the complete journey, calculating each leg's time separately. Equal uphill and downhill distances allow a convenient representative one-way distance.
questions.methodNote: Page 36 defines speed as distance divided by time. Page 37 explains average speed and Example 28 divides distance by a fractional time. Page 38 applies speed, distance and time relationships.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine unequal journey times over equal distances to calculate the average speed of the whole trip.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that the descending boundary has horizontal and vertical totals equal to the overall width and height, without finding individual step lengths.

questions.mappingNote: Apply the taught boundary-sum method, recognising that the staircase's rightward segments together equal the bottom width and its downward segments together equal the left height.
questions.methodNote: Page 10 defines perimeter as the sum of boundary side lengths. Page 11 Example 7 adds the horizontal and vertical side lengths of a rectilinear figure.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise that the descending boundary has horizontal and vertical totals equal to the overall width and height, without finding individual step lengths.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify inferred dimensions and calculate the same composite area using both addition and subtraction.

questions.mappingNote: The task explicitly requires two methods for one composite figure. Adding component square and triangle areas and subtracting missing triangles from an enclosing square directly apply the inspected teaching.
questions.methodNote: Pages 13–14 teach rectangle and square area. Pages 17–18 teach finding composite areas by addition and subtraction. Pages 21–24 establish triangle area using perpendicular base and height, with Example 18 combining rectangle and triangle areas.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify inferred dimensions and calculate the same composite area using both addition and subtraction.

classification.difficultyReason: Find different rectangular arrangements of 16 unit tiles and compare their perimeters.

questions.mappingNote: Arrange 16 unit tiles using whole-number factor pairs, then add the four sides of each rectangle. Comparing perimeters for a fixed area is the directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 13 relates rectangle area to unit-square counting and the product of adjacent side lengths. Pages 10–11 calculate perimeter by adding every boundary side.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find different rectangular arrangements of 16 unit tiles and compare their perimeters.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate the fixed perimeter into adjacent sides summing to 12, systematically enumerate whole-number pairs, and compare their areas to establish both extremes.

questions.mappingNote: Enumerate whole-number adjacent side pairs with sum 12, draw the rectangles and multiply their dimensions. Comparing areas for a common perimeter is the directly assessed investigation; no algebraic optimisation is needed.
questions.methodNote: Pages 10–11 calculate perimeter by adding boundary lengths. Page 13 calculates rectangle area by multiplying adjacent side lengths; page 14 treats a square as a rectangle with equal sides.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Investigate rectangles with a fixed perimeter, calculate their areas and identify the extreme areas for whole-number side lengths.

classification.difficultyReason: Explore dimensions with a fixed area, compare their perimeters and identify the minimum without restricting dimensions to whole numbers.

questions.mappingNote: Find dimension pairs with product 64, calculate their perimeters and compare them. The directly assessed skill is comparing perimeters of rectangles with the same area. No whole-number restriction is introduced.
questions.methodNote: Page 10 defines perimeter as the sum of side lengths; Example 7 on page 11 demonstrates adding boundary lengths. Page 13 gives rectangle area as length multiplied by width.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Explore dimensions with a fixed area, compare their perimeters and identify the minimum without restricting dimensions to whole numbers.

classification.difficultyReason: Explore rectangle dimensions with a fixed perimeter and identify the maximum area without restricting side lengths to whole numbers.

questions.mappingNote: Use the fencing length to obtain a fixed sum of adjacent rectangle sides, explore products of compatible dimensions, and identify the square as the maximum-area rectangle.
questions.methodNote: Pages 10–11 calculate perimeter by adding boundary side lengths. Page 13 defines rectangle area as length multiplied by width; page 14 applies the same formula to squares.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Explore rectangle dimensions with a fixed perimeter and identify the maximum area without restricting side lengths to whole numbers.
